summary.text: Introduce companion sequences \(c_0=1,c_1=-2\) and \(s_0=0,s_1=2\), both satisfying \(x_{n+2}=-4x_{n+1}-64x_n\), and prove \(2a_n=4\cdot8^n-4(-8)^n+c_{n+1}\), together with \(c_{2k}=c_k^2-15s_k^2\) and \(c_k^2+15s_k^2=64^k\). At \(n=2m+1\), these identities give \(2a_{2m+1}=64^{m+1}+c_{2m+2}=2c_{m+1}^2\), hence \(a_{2m+1}=c_{m+1}^2\).

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the integer sequence defined by
\[
a_0=-1,\qquad a_1=4,\qquad a_2=176,\qquad a_3=3136,
\]
and, for every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
a_{n+4}=-4a_{n+3}+256a_{n+1}+4096a_n. \tag{1}
\]
We prove that for every nonnegative integer \(n\), the odd-indexed term \(a_{2n+1}\) is a square.

Define two auxiliary integer sequences \((c_n)\) and \((s_n)\) by
\[
c_0=1,\qquad c_1=-2,\qquad c_{n+2}=-4c_{n+1}-64c_n, \tag{2}
\]
and
\[
s_0=0,\qquad s_1=2,\qquad s_{n+2}=-4s_{n+1}-64s_n. \tag{3}
\]
We will ultimately prove the more precise formula
\[
a_{2n+1}=c_{n+1}^2. \tag{4}
\]

First we obtain a useful expression for every term of \(a\).

**Lemma 1.** For every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
2a_n=4\cdot 8^n-4\cdot(-8)^n+c_{n+1}. \tag{5}
\]

To prove this, set
\[
B_n=4\cdot 8^n-4\cdot(-8)^n+c_{n+1}.
\]
We show that both \(B_n\) and \(2a_n\) obey the same fourth-order recurrence and have the same first four values.

The characteristic polynomial associated with (1) is
\[
P(x)=x^4+4x^3-256x-4096.
\]
Both \(8\) and \(-8\) are roots of this polynomial. Indeed,
\[
8^4+4\cdot 8^3-256\cdot 8-4096
=4096+2048-2048-4096=0,
\]
and
\[
(-8)^4+4(-8)^3-256(-8)-4096
=4096-2048+2048-4096=0.
\]
Consequently, each of the sequences \(8^n\) and \((-8)^n\) satisfies
\[
u_{n+4}=-4u_{n+3}+256u_{n+1}+4096u_n. \tag{6}
\]

The shifted sequence \(c_{n+1}\) also satisfies (6). In fact, applying (2) twice gives
\[
c_{n+5}+4c_{n+4}=-64c_{n+3}.
\]
Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
&c_{n+5}+4c_{n+4}-256c_{n+2}-4096c_{n+1}\\
&\qquad=-64c_{n+3}-256c_{n+2}-4096c_{n+1}\\
&\qquad=-64\bigl(c_{n+3}+4c_{n+2}+64c_{n+1}\bigr)=0,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the final equality is another instance of (2). Thus
\[
c_{n+5}=-4c_{n+4}+256c_{n+2}+4096c_{n+1},
\]
which is precisely (6) for the shifted sequence. By linearity, \(B_n\) satisfies the same recurrence.

On the other hand, multiplying (1) by \(2\) shows that \(2a_n\) satisfies this recurrence as well. It remains to compare four initial terms. From (2),
\[
c_2=-4(-2)-64(1)=-56,
\]
\[
c_3=-4(-56)-64(-2)=352,
\]
and
\[
c_4=-4(352)-64(-56)=2176.
\]
Therefore,
\[
B_0=4-4+c_1=-2=2a_0,
\]
\[
B_1=4\cdot8-4(-8)+c_2=32+32-56=8=2a_1,
\]
\[
B_2=4\cdot64-4\cdot64+c_3=352=2a_2,
\]
and
\[
B_3=4\cdot512-4(-512)+c_4=2048+2048+2176=6272=2a_3.
\]
Two sequences satisfying the same recurrence of order four and agreeing at indices \(0,1,2,3\) agree everywhere: this follows immediately by induction, because agreement through index \(n+3\) forces agreement at index \(n+4\) via the recurrence. Thus (5) holds for all \(n\).

We next establish identities relating \(c_n\) and \(s_n\).

**Lemma 2 (one-step formulas).** For every \(m\ge 0\),
\[
c_{m+1}=-2c_m-30s_m, \tag{7}
\]
\[
s_{m+1}=2c_m-2s_m. \tag{8}
\]

For \(m=0\), these are simply
\[
c_1=-2=-2c_0-30s_0
\]
and
\[
s_1=2=2c_0-2s_0.
\]
Suppose (7) and (8) hold at an index \(m\). Using (2) and the induction hypotheses,
\[
\begin{aligned}
c_{m+2}
&=-4c_{m+1}-64c_m\\
&=-4(-2c_m-30s_m)-64c_m\\
&=-56c_m+120s_m.
\end{aligned}
\]
Meanwhile,
\[
\begin{aligned}
-2c_{m+1}-30s_{m+1}
&=-2(-2c_m-30s_m)-30(2c_m-2s_m)\\
&=-56c_m+120s_m.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus (7) holds at \(m+1\). Similarly, by (3),
\[
\begin{aligned}
s_{m+2}
&=-4s_{m+1}-64s_m\\
&=-4(2c_m-2s_m)-64s_m\\
&=-8c_m-56s_m,
\end{aligned}
\]
while
\[
\begin{aligned}
2c_{m+1}-2s_{m+1}
&=2(-2c_m-30s_m)-2(2c_m-2s_m)\\
&=-8c_m-56s_m.
\end{aligned}
\]
So (8) also holds at \(m+1\). Induction proves both formulas.

**Lemma 3 (addition formulas).** For all nonnegative integers \(m,n\),
\[
c_{m+n}=c_mc_n-15s_ms_n, \tag{9}
\]
and
\[
s_{m+n}=c_ms_n+s_mc_n. \tag{10}
\]

Fix \(m\) and induct on \(n\). At \(n=0\), the formulas follow from \(c_0=1\) and \(s_0=0\):
\[
c_m=c_m c_0-15s_m s_0,
\qquad
s_m=c_m s_0+s_m c_0.
\]
Suppose (9) and (10) hold for a given \(n\). Applying (7) at index \(m+n\), followed by the induction hypotheses, yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
c_{m+n+1}
&=-2c_{m+n}-30s_{m+n}\\
&=-2(c_mc_n-15s_ms_n)-30(c_ms_n+s_mc_n)\\
&=c_m(-2c_n-30s_n)-15s_m(2c_n-2s_n)\\
&=c_mc_{n+1}-15s_ms_{n+1},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the last line uses (7) and (8) at index \(n\). Likewise, applying (8) at index \(m+n\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
s_{m+n+1}
&=2c_{m+n}-2s_{m+n}\\
&=2(c_mc_n-15s_ms_n)-2(c_ms_n+s_mc_n)\\
&=c_m(2c_n-2s_n)+s_m(-2c_n-30s_n)\\
&=c_ms_{n+1}+s_mc_{n+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus both addition formulas follow by induction.

**Lemma 4 (norm identity).** For every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
c_n^2+15s_n^2=64^n. \tag{11}
\]

At \(n=0\), the left side is \(1^2+15\cdot0^2=1=64^0\). Suppose (11) holds at \(n\). From the one-step formulas,
\[
\begin{aligned}
c_{n+1}^2+15s_{n+1}^2
&=(-2c_n-30s_n)^2+15(2c_n-2s_n)^2\\
&=\bigl(4c_n^2+120c_ns_n+900s_n^2\bigr)\\
&\quad+15\bigl(4c_n^2-8c_ns_n+4s_n^2\bigr)\\
&=64c_n^2+960s_n^2\\
&=64(c_n^2+15s_n^2)\\
&=64\cdot64^n=64^{n+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (11) by induction.

We now evaluate an odd-indexed term. Fix \(n\ge 0\), and put
\[
r=n+1.
\]
Applying Lemma 1 at index \(2n+1\), we have
\[
2a_{2n+1}=4\cdot8^{2n+1}-4\cdot(-8)^{2n+1}+c_{2n+2}. \tag{12}
\]
Since
\[
8^{2n+1}=8(8^2)^n=8\cdot64^n
\]
and
\[
(-8)^{2n+1}=-8\bigl((-8)^2\bigr)^n=-8\cdot64^n,
\]
the two exponential terms in (12) combine as follows:
\[
4\cdot8^{2n+1}-4\cdot(-8)^{2n+1}
=32\cdot64^n+32\cdot64^n
=64^{n+1}=64^r. \tag{13}
\]
Also, \(2n+2=2r=r+r\). Taking \(m=n=r\) in the addition formula (9) gives
\[
c_{2r}=c_r^2-15s_r^2. \tag{14}
\]
The norm identity (11) gives
\[
64^r=c_r^2+15s_r^2. \tag{15}
\]
Substituting (13), (14), and (15) into (12), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
2a_{2n+1}
&=64^r+c_{2r}\\
&=(c_r^2+15s_r^2)+(c_r^2-15s_r^2)\\
&=2c_r^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Because these are integers and \(2\ne0\), cancellation of the factor \(2\) yields
\[
a_{2n+1}=c_r^2=c_{n+1}^2.
\]
Thus \(a_{2n+1}\) is the square of the integer \(c_{n+1}\) for every nonnegative integer \(n\), proving the conjecture.
